cultivar: Anhua and other Hunan medium- and large-leaf population bushes
processing: Post-fermented and hand-compressed: steamed grade-2 to 3 Anhua hei mao cha (pan-fired, rolled, pile-fermented, pine-fire dried) is packed into a long bamboo-strip basket lined with liao leaves and palm fibre and compressed by a team of men stamping and tightening the basket with wooden levers; the finished log, about 36 kg and 1.5 m long, is stood outside for around seven weeks to dry in sun, wind and dew.
harvest_season: Grade-2 to 3 leaf from spring and summer; logs are made in the hot months (roughly June to September) when outdoor drying is possible.
appearance_dry: A huge bamboo-wrapped cylinder; cut open, a dense dark-brown tea core sometimes speckled with golden flowers, sold as whole logs or sawn into discs a centimetre or two thick.
appearance_wet: Coarse dark-brown leaves and stems, softened but still firm.
taste_profile: Thick, sweet and woody with pine smoke, a bamboo-leaf freshness from the wrapping and a long, cooling finish; aged logs add jujube and a mushroom-like softness.

brewing.notes: Saw or chip off a piece, rinse once, boiling water in a clay pot or gaiwan; even better simmered 5–10 minutes in a kettle. Keep a disc in its bamboo leaf and it will go on ageing.

vintage_note: Sold by the year the log was made, as whole logs (a collector's item that takes two people to lift), as sawn discs of a few hundred grams, or as the smaller Bai Liang (about 3.6 kg) and Shi Liang (about 360 g) versions. Logs from the late-1990s revival to the current year are on the market; 5–15 years is the usual drinking window, and the discs are what most people actually buy.
description:
Qian Liang Cha is the biggest unit of tea anyone makes: a bamboo-wrapped log of Anhua dark tea about a metre and a half long and 36 kilos in weight, 'a thousand taels' in the old measure. It is also called Hua Juan, 'flower roll', after the pattern the bamboo weave leaves on the tea. It was made in Anhua from the mid-nineteenth century for the trade to the north-west, stopped in 1958 because it took too many men and too long, and came back in small numbers in the 1980s and commercially from the late 1990s. Today it is the showpiece of Hunan dark tea.

Making one is a team sport. Steamed hei mao cha is packed by the kilo into a long basket of bamboo strips lined with liao leaves and palm fibre, and a crew of men stamp, roll and tighten the basket with wooden levers while chanting to keep time, until the tea is compressed into a solid cylinder. The log is then stood outside for around seven weeks to dry in sun, wind and night dew, which is when the character develops; golden flowers sometimes grow naturally inside. Nobody can tell you what a log is like until it is cut.

In the cup it is thick, sweet and woody, with pine smoke from the raw material, a bamboo-leaf freshness from the wrapping and a long, cooling finish; aged logs add jujube and a soft mushroom note. Saw or chip off a piece, rinse once and brew with boiling water, and it will give ten steeps; simmering a chunk for ten minutes gives the fullest cup. It is a winter tea and a tea for a crowd.

Whole logs are sold by the year of making, mostly to shops and collectors who stand them in a corner and saw off discs to order; most drinkers buy the discs, each wrapped in its bamboo leaf, or the smaller Bai Liang and Shi Liang versions of the same tea. Baishaxi is the historic maker and many Anhua factories now follow. Check that a disc smells sweet and smoky rather than musty, and that the bamboo wrapping is intact, because the wrapping is part of how the tea ages.

If you buy one disc, buy a second to put away: the difference between a five- and a fifteen-year log is the whole argument for ageing dark tea.
history:
Qian Liang grew out of an older, smaller log. Shaanxi merchants were already making a cylindrical Bai Liang, 'hundred tael' tea, in Anhua by about the start of the Daoguang era, and in the Tongzhi reign Shanxi merchants scaled the idea up with more leaf and stronger pressing; the firm is named San He He in one account and San He Gong in another. The result weighed 1,000 old taels, about 36.25 kg, and it took its name from that.

Chinese tea histories commonly give a halt in 1958 and a revival by 1997, with an intermediate run in the 1980s, though the details vary. The craft is now national intangible heritage.
